claims.text: Rapid quenching locks in a metastable nanostructure.
Rapid quenching locks in a defect-rich nanostructure.
Rapid quenching produces a homogeneously alloyed Pt–Pd–Au–Ag–Cu nanostructure.
The defect-rich quenched structure provides more catalytic active sites than a slow-cooled structure.
The additional active sites enhance catalytic performance, including oxygen-reduction performance.
The precursor is a uniform solution containing Pt, Pd, Au, Ag, and Cu salts.
Rapid quenching prevents the nanoparticle system from reaching equilibrium.
Quenching freezes a high density of defects, grain boundaries, and lattice strain into the nanoparticles.
Defects, grain boundaries, and lattice strain serve as catalytic active sites.
These structural features enhance electron-transfer and adsorption/desorption steps in catalytic reactions.
Slow cooling permits defect annealing and atomic rearrangement toward equilibrium.
Slow-cooled nanoparticles have lower defect densities and reduced catalytic performance relative to rapidly quenched nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit broader XRD peaks than the slow-cooled baseline.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit higher defect densities by high-resolution TEM than the slow-cooled baseline.
The structural features induced by quenching will correlate with increased turnover frequency.
The structural features induced by quenching will correlate with improved stability during oxygen reduction.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal HEA nanoparticles synthesized near 500 °C under inert atmospheres when quenching kinetics dominate.
Excessive defect density may become detrimental to catalytic performance.
